paras: The Cole City convict mine shooting took place on July 24, 1903, when state guards at the Dade County coal mines at Cole City (also spelled Coal City), Georgia, fired on Black convicts who had refused to come out of the mine at the change of shifts. Early wire reports said two convicts were fatally wounded, but a later Atlanta account named three wounded men, Joe Beck, "Snaps" Jordan and an unnamed convict, and reported no deaths. Newspapers across the country carried the story as a convict "mutiny," and the Savannah Tribune printed a version of it on its front page.

The mines belonged to the Georgia Iron and Coal Company and were worked by about 200 Georgia convicts leased to the company, 125 of them on the day shift. A Chattanooga dispatch described most of the convicts as "negroes" and said some were serving life sentences. Deputy Warden J. D. Goode was in charge of the camp for the state, and according to the Savannah Tribune the company's president was Joel Hurt.

According to the wire, the trouble began over the punishment of a convict for breaking the rules, and when the day shift heard of it, its men refused to leave the mine at the change of shifts. Goode telegraphed the state prison commission that 125 men "refuse to come out," and Chairman J. S. Turner replied that he should be firm but patient and avoid bloodshed while Warden Jake Moore traveled to the camp. Before Moore arrived, shortly before 6 o'clock by the Tribune's account, convicts in the front ranks "hurled epithets and missiles" at the guards, who fired into them.

The next day the prison commission knew the shot men only by their numbers, as ringleaders, and said the guards had been "forced to fire." The Atlanta Constitution later gave a fuller version: Henry Lowe, who had cursed a guard, refused to be whipped and rushed Goode with a heavy piece of timber, and 125 convicts joined him. Five guards then fired, shooting off Joe Beck's cheek with buckshot, wounding "Snaps" Jordan in the leg and hitting a third man in the breast.

After the mutiny was over, Lowe and another convict were whipped, and the convicts were put on bread and water and threatened with no food at all. Thirty-nine Black convicts were moved to the furnace at Rising Fawn and the guard was strengthened, and on Sunday Turner and Moore told the convicts that discipline would be kept "at any cost." The convicts, some in chains, then went back to work. No report of an inquest, an investigation of the shooting or the wounded men's later condition appears in the coverage.

On July 25 the Chattanooga dispatch ran in Montgomery, Savannah, Indianapolis and Butte papers under headlines such as "Convicts in Mutiny" and "Fired on Convicts." Shorter versions ran in Washington, Raleigh, the Georgia weekly Dawson News and Midwestern digest columns into early August. In the retelling, "probably fatally wounded" often became deaths: the Butte paper's headline said "Two Are Killed," a Tennessee weekly's said "Two Killed," and Minneapolis and South Dakota digests said "Two negroes were shot dead."

Every account came from the guards, the prison commission or the company, calling the convicts "desperate characters" and "ringleaders," and none quoted a convict. The Constitution's headline, "Beck and Jordan Were Shot Down Quelling the Disturbance," presented the shooting, the whippings and the bread-and-water diet as the "vigorous measures" that ended the mutiny.

The Savannah Tribune, a Black weekly, ran the story on its front page on August 1 under the headline "Convicts Are Shot." Its text was the same syndicated story the Gainesville Star in Florida had printed four days earlier, including the subhead "Desperate Men at Bay." The Tribune added no comment and did not name the wounded men.

The papers disagreed on how many men were shot and whether any died: the wire said two were probably fatally wounded, digests said two were shot dead, and the Constitution listed three wounded and no deaths. The Constitution's version came later and from officials at the camp; no later report of a death was found.

bases: State guards at a convict-lease mine fired on convicts in their custody who refused an order to come out of the mine (A1, A10).

The Chattanooga wire (A1), the Atlanta prison-commission reports (A2, A7) and the Atlanta Constitution's later account (A10) agree that guards shot convicts at Cole City on July 24, though they differ on the number shot and whether any died.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Convicts in Mutiny', 'Fired on Convicts', 'Convicts Defy the Guards'; convicts called 'desperate characters' and 'belligerents', the guards' firing presented as restoring order.
The Constitution's 'Beck and Jordan Were Shot Down Quelling the Disturbance' presented the shooting, whippings and bread-and-water diet as 'vigorous measures' that ended the mutiny.
The Savannah Tribune ran the syndicated 'Convicts Are Shot' text, including 'desperate men at bay', on its front page without comment.
